questions.q: Aryabhata found π with four steps of arithmetic. What are the steps, and what value do they give?
questions.do: Read Idea 2 · Ganitapada 10, “π from four steps of arithmetic”.
questions.a: Add 4 to 100, multiply by 8, add 62,000: (100 + 4) × 8 + 62,000 = 62,832. That is the circumference of a circle 20,000 across, so π ≈ 62,832 ÷ 20,000 = 3.1416. He called it approximate; it is too big by only 0.0000073, about 2 parts in a million.

questions.q: Using Aryabhata's rotation period, which launch site gives an eastbound rocket the most free speed, and which gives the least?
questions.do: In Idea 1, click each launch-site button (Sriharikota, Kourou, Boca Chica, Kennedy, Baikonur) and read the free speed.
questions.a: Most: Kourou at 5.24° N, 0.463 km/s. Least: Baikonur at 45.96° N, 0.323 km/s. Sriharikota gives 0.452 km/s. Sites nearer the equator move faster as the Earth turns.

questions.q: Aryabhata's sine table was good enough for the naked eye. Is it good enough to aim a spacecraft at Mars?
questions.do: In Idea 3 · Dasagitika 12, read the Test / Result table and the verdict under it.
questions.a: No. His worst error is about 1.7 arc-minutes, close to the sharpest a human eye can see. But aiming at Mars with it would miss by up to 112,005 km, about 16.5 Mars diameters.

questions.q: Aryabhata said eclipses are shadows, not a demon. Why can the Moon be fully hidden in a lunar eclipse?
questions.do: Read the similar-triangles result at the end of Idea 4 · Golapada 5 and 37.
questions.a: The Earth's shadow is about 1,381,349 km long, 3.6 times the Moon's distance. Where the Moon crosses it, the shadow is still about 9,196 km wide, wider than the Moon (3,475 km). So the Moon can sit fully inside it, and total lunar eclipses happen.

questions.q: From his yuga counts, how long did Aryabhata say the Earth takes to turn once against the stars, and how close is that to the modern value?
questions.do: In Idea 1, read the table One turn against the stars.
questions.a: Aryabhata: 86,164.101 s (23 h 56 m 4.10 s). Modern atomic-clock value: 86,164.091 s (23 h 56 m 4.09 s). The difference is only 0.011 s, 1 part in about 8 million. It comes from 1,582,237,500 Earth turns in a yuga of 4,320,000 years.
